intro.html: Two uncomfortable feelings share this topic. Regret comes from knowing you did wrong: you feel sorry and want to make it right. Embarrassment comes from being seen doing something silly: your face goes red and you wish you could disappear.

Sorry for a wrong: remorse, contrite, penitent, compunction, rueful, and the verb atone (make up for it). Embarrassed: sheepish and abashed (mild), chagrin (embarrassed and annoyed), mortified (deeply embarrassed).
Several of these words hold sharp Latin pictures: remorse is a wrong that keeps biting you, contrite means crushed, and compunction is a prick of guilt, like a pin.

words.def: deep, painful regret for having done wrong
words.ex: Filled with {remorse}, Kai gave back the toy he had taken and apologized to his little brother.
words.ctx: The vandal showed no {remorse} in court; he smirked through the whole hearing and never once apologized to the shop owner whose window he had smashed.
words.etym: From Latin remordere, “to bite again”: re- (again) + mordere (to bite). Remorse is a wrong that keeps biting you.

mn.text: Kai broke his brother’s toy truck, and the guilt keeps biting at him all evening until he hands over his own teddy bear; that biting regret is {remorse}.

scene.alt: A sorry boy kneels and gives his teddy bear to his crying little brother beside a broken toy wagon.

words.def: truly sorry for having done wrong
words.ex: The {contrite} puppy crept out from under the table after chewing Dad’s slipper.
words.ctx: At first Dev insisted the broken window was not his fault, but by dinner he was {contrite}, offering to pay for the glass from his own savings.
words.etym: From Latin contritus, “crushed,” from conterere (to grind, to crush): a contrite person feels crushed by guilt.

mn.text: After chewing Dad’s slipper to bits, Rufus creeps over with his ears down and lays it at Dad’s feet; the crushed, sorry pup is {contrite}.

scene.alt: A sad puppy lies with its ears down beside a chewed slipper, apologizing to its owner.

words.def: sorry for doing wrong and wanting to make up for it
words.ex: The {penitent} boy swept up every bit of the vase he had knocked over.
words.ctx: Unlike his brother, who shrugged off the scolding, Sam was {penitent}: he apologized to the neighbor and offered to mow her lawn for a month.
words.etym: From Latin paenitens, “regretting,” from paenitere (to regret).

mn.text: After breaking Granny’s teapot, Pip takes a pen and writes “Sorry!” ten times on a big card, then offers to wash her dishes all week; he is {penitent}.

scene.alt: A sorry boy hands his grandmother a card that says sorry, next to the teapot he broke.

words.def: showing regret, often with a sad or wry smile
words.ex: With a {rueful} grin, Grandpa admitted he had locked the keys in the car again.
words.ctx: Looking at the blackened cookies, Nell gave a {rueful} laugh: she had set the timer for twenty minutes instead of ten, and there was no one to blame but herself.
words.etym: From Middle English rewful: rewe (sorrow, pity) + -ful.

mn.text: Pip kicks his new ball right onto the roof, then looks up with a sorry little half smile: “Oops.” That regretful look is {rueful}.

scene.alt: A boy scratches his head with a sorry half smile, looking up at the ball he kicked onto a roof.

words.def: a twinge of guilt or doubt that stops or follows a wrong act
words.ex: The raccoon ate the whole pie without the slightest {compunction}.
words.ctx: Lila felt no {compunction} about pointing out the error on the board, but later she felt a pang of guilt when she saw how embarrassed her teacher looked.
words.etym: From Latin compungere, “to prick hard, to sting”: com- (thoroughly) + pungere (to prick).
words.note: It is most often used with no or without: “He took the last slice without compunction” means he felt no guilt at all.

mn.text: Reaching for her sister’s candy, Ivy feels a little prick of guilt, sharp as a cactus needle, and pulls her hand back; that twinge is {compunction}.

scene.alt: A girl reaches for her sister’s candy jar, then pauses with a twinge of guilt.

words.def: to make up for a wrong one has done
words.ex: To {atone} for forgetting her birthday, Sami baked his sister a three-layer cake.
words.ctx: Having missed three practices, the goalie tried to {atone} for his absence by arriving early every day and staying late to pick up the cones.
words.etym: From the phrase at one, “in harmony”: to atone first meant to become friends again.

mn.cue: AT ONE again: make it up
mn.text: Kai broke Lila’s kite, so he spends his whole Saturday building her a new one; he wants to {atone} for the wrong and be at one with her again.

cast.say: I made you a new one!

scene.alt: A boy gives a girl a new kite he built to make up for breaking hers, and she cheers.

words.def: annoyance mixed with embarrassment, often after a failure
words.ex: To his {chagrin}, Felix discovered he had worn mismatched shoes to the job interview.
words.ctx: Much to the chef’s {chagrin}, the judges praised his rival’s simple soup and barely tasted the fancy dessert he had worked on all week.

mn.text: Felix slips in a puddle right in front of the whole bus stop, gets up red-faced and cross, and forces a shaky grin; that sour, embarrassed feeling is {chagrin}.

scene.alt: A man who just slipped in a puddle covers his eyes, red-faced and annoyed, as a girl laughs.

words.ex: Lin was {mortified} when her phone rang loudly in the middle of the school play.
words.ctx: Jamal had bragged all week about his cooking, so he was {mortified} when his guests politely pushed the salty stew aside and asked if anyone wanted to order pizza.
words.etym: From mortify, from Latin mortificare, “to put to death”: to be mortified is to feel you could die of embarrassment.

mn.cue: MORT = death: could DIE of shame
mn.text: When Lin’s phone blares a quacking ringtone in the silent theater, she wishes the floor would swallow her; she is {mortified}.

scene.alt: A woman blushes in horror as her phone rings in a quiet theater, while others glare and shush her.

words.ex: Caught singing at the top of his lungs in the shower, Dev came out looking {abashed}.
words.ctx: Jonah, usually so bold, stood {abashed} before the principal, staring at his shoes and mumbling that he had not meant to start the food fight.

mn.text: Caught with frosting on his nose after sneaking a taste of the birthday cake, Pip turns red and stares at his shoes, as bashful as can be; he is {abashed}.

scene.alt: A boy with frosting on his nose hides his face in embarrassment while his mother grins at him.

words.def: embarrassed from knowing one has done something silly
words.ex: Grandpa gave a {sheepish} smile when he found his glasses on top of his head.
words.ctx: After insisting that the remote was broken, Dad wore a {sheepish} grin when we pointed out that he had forgotten to put the batteries in.
words.etym: From sheep + -ish; at first it meant meek and timid, like a sheep.

mn.text: The sheep tries to jump the fence, lands in the pigs’ mud instead, and looks up with an embarrassed little grin; it looks {sheepish}.

scene.alt: A sheep with a muddy, embarrassed grin stands in a mud puddle while a pig laughs.

head: word
feeling
strength
rows: embarrassed enough to want to vanish
sorry and ready to make up for it
guilt that will not stop biting
after.cap: Embarrassment and regret, from mild to strong.

after.html: You will often meet compunction in the negative: someone who acts without compunction or with no compunction feels no guilt at all. And to atone is what a penitent person does: make up for the wrong.

items.q: “The squirrel raided the bird feeder without compunction.” This means the squirrel…
items.why: Compunction is a twinge of guilt, so without compunction means with no guilt at all.
Chagrin is the sour, irritated embarrassment you feel after a failure, like losing to a rival you had mocked.

items.q: The verb atone comes from the English phrase…
items.why: To atone was once to be “at one” again, reconciled. Today it means to make up for a wrong.
mort means death, as in mortal. To be mortified is to feel you could die of embarrassment.
